prompt:
A 34-year-old woman with chronic hypertension, obesity (BMI 36), and prediabetes stopped her oral contraceptive last month because she and her partner want to conceive. She takes lisinopril 20 mg, chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg (started for LDL 170 mg/dL and a strong family history), and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg most days for migraines. Home blood pressure averages 138/88. Creatinine is normal and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 45 mg/g. Her only prior pregnancy was complicated by preeclampsia with delivery at 34 weeks. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She asks how her medications should change before and during pregnancy. How would you manage her?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Stop lisinopril now while she is attempting conception because ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic.
Switch to labetalol or extended-release nifedipine as pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive therapy.
Stop atorvastatin while she is attempting conception and during pregnancy.
Confirm a negative pregnancy test before finalizing the medication changes and repeat if menses are missed.
Recommend low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily starting at 12 to 16 weeks of gestation for preeclampsia prevention.
Start a prenatal vitamin containing at least 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before conception.
Target blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg during pregnancy.
Reassess home and clinic blood pressure within 2 to 4 weeks after the medication switch.
Instruct her to contact the clinic promptly after a positive pregnancy test to begin early prenatal care.
Refer to maternal-fetal medicine for preconception counseling given chronic hypertension and prior preeclampsia.
Obtain baseline platelet count, creatinine, liver enzymes, and quantified urine protein early in pregnancy.
Replace daily ibuprofen with acetaminophen and nonpharmacologic migraine strategies, avoiding NSAIDs in pregnancy.
Check hemoglobin A1c before conception or screen for diabetes early in pregnancy given obesity and prediabetes.
Counsel on nutrition and physical activity to support weight reduction before conception.
Counsel on preeclampsia warning symptoms including severe headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, and blood pressure of 160/110 or higher.
Consider tapering chlorthalidone during pregnancy unless it is needed for blood pressure control.
Review migraine prophylaxis options that are compatible with pregnancy if attacks remain frequent.
Advise waiting to conceive until blood pressure is controlled on the new regimen, using barrier contraception in the interim.
Plan postpartum follow-up for long-term cardiovascular risk and resumption of statin therapy after breastfeeding.
Counsel that labetalol, nifedipine, and postpartum enalapril are compatible with breastfeeding.
Continue lisinopril throughout pregnancy for renal protection because of albuminuria.
Switch lisinopril to losartan.
Switch lisinopril to aliskiren.
Start atenolol as the preferred beta-blocker for pregnancy.
Add spironolactone for blood pressure control during pregnancy.
Continue atorvastatin throughout pregnancy.
Prescribe aspirin 325 mg daily starting at conception.
Delay aspirin until the third trimester.
Continue daily ibuprofen for migraines during pregnancy.
Prescribe a daily butalbital-containing or opioid combination for migraines.
Start valproate for migraine prophylaxis.
Escalate antihypertensives to keep diastolic blood pressure below 70 mm Hg in pregnancy.
Stop all antihypertensives once pregnant in anticipation of the physiologic blood pressure decline.
Use oral hydralazine monotherapy as the long-term first-line antihypertensive.
Recommend bed rest during pregnancy to prevent preeclampsia.
Recommend calorie restriction for weight loss during pregnancy.
Start topiramate for migraine prevention and weight loss.
Prescribe ergotamine for migraine attacks during pregnancy.
Start phentermine-topiramate or a GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight loss while attempting conception.
Recommend vitamin C and vitamin E supplementation to prevent preeclampsia.
